article_title: Upward Bound Math-Science Program: Description and Interim Impact Estimates
citation: Robert B. Olsen, Neil Seftor, Tim Silva, David Myers, David DesRoches, Julie Young. (2007). Upward Bound Math-Science Program: Description and Interim Impact Estimates. Washington, DC: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Hands-on math-science exposure pattern: labs, computer facilities, field sites, and scientist contact
description: The UBMS design pattern combines practical STEM settings with expert contact: grantees "provide participants with hands-on experience in laboratories, computer facilities, and at field sites, as well as opportunities to learn from mathematicians and scientists at host institutions." The report presents this as the program's core design for building skills and experiences that prepare disadvantaged students for college success in math and science fields.
requirements: Host institutions (colleges and universities) with laboratories, computer facilities, and field sites
Access to mathematicians and scientists at host institutions
constraints: Implemented within the federal Upward Bound grant structure for disadvantaged high school students
target_learning_goals: Math and science preparation for college
Career exposure to mathematicians and scientists
examples: By 2004, 127 UBMS projects operated at colleges and universities serving nearly 7,000 students
key_sources: Robert B. Olsen, Neil Seftor, Tim Silva, David Myers, David DesRoches, Julie Young. (2007). Upward Bound Math-Science Program: Description and Interim Impact Estimates. Washington, DC: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/upward-bound-mathscience-program-description-and-interim-impact-estimates

article_title: From fear to innovation: A case study of transformative faculty development for ethical AI integration in higher education
citation: John Chick, Laura Morello and Stephanie Staffey. (2026). From fear to innovation: a case study of transformative faculty development for ethical AI integration in higher education. International Journal for Educational Integrity. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40979-026-00225-x
title: UBRIDGE Institute: a six-week synchronous interdisciplinary faculty development program for ethical AI integration
description: The UBRIDGE (Universal design, Bloom's taxonomy, Reflection, Integration, Design thinking, Growth mindset, Ethics) Institute was a six-session synchronous Zoom program, two hours weekly, for interdisciplinary faculty across arts, sciences, education and health professions. It aimed to scaffold AI integration through "inclusive pedagogy, ethical reasoning, and course redesign principles". Sessions combined hands-on AI experimentation, design-thinking worksheets, discussion boards, and capstone AI-integration plans.
requirements: Voluntary participation with sustained six-session duration, active learning, coherence with participant needs, and collective participation, following Darling-Hammond et al. as the article cites
constraints: Self-selection bias: participants volunteered and received modest stipends, limiting generalizability to faculty who might resist such opportunities
target_learners: Higher education faculty and staff across disciplines, from novice to experienced AI users
examples: Participants produced capstone projects ranging from redesigned assignments leveraging AI to departmental policy proposals and research projects examining AI impact
key_sources: John Chick, Laura Morello and Stephanie Staffey. (2026). From fear to innovation: a case study of transformative faculty development for ethical AI integration in higher education. International Journal for Educational Integrity. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40979-026-00225-x

article_title: From fear to innovation: A case study of transformative faculty development for ethical AI integration in higher education
citation: John Chick, Laura Morello and Stephanie Staffey. (2026). From fear to innovation: a case study of transformative faculty development for ethical AI integration in higher education. International Journal for Educational Integrity. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40979-026-00225-x
title: Integrated theoretical framework combining UDL, Bloom's Taxonomy, and design thinking for AI-focused faculty development
description: The institute design rested on three complementary lenses treated as interconnected rather than separate: Universal Design for Learning as the inclusive framework, Bloom's Taxonomy as a cognitive framework for judging AI's appropriate roles across cognitive levels, and design thinking's five stages (empathize, define, ideate, prototype, test) as the innovation process. The article states the design "emphasized their interconnection through three primary theoretical lenses", using Bloom to help faculty "discern when AI collaboration enhances versus undermines learning objectives across cognitive levels".
requirements: Faculty development must address multiple dimensions simultaneously: technical competence, pedagogical innovation, ethical reasoning, disciplinary application, and institutional navigation
constraints: AI's role in higher-order thinking remains contested territory requiring careful pedagogical consideration, per the article
target_learners: Higher education faculty integrating AI into teaching
target_learning_goals: Judging appropriate AI roles across cognitive levels
examples: Sessions moved participants from lower-order engagement (remembering AI capabilities) to higher-order application (evaluating ethical dimensions, creating innovative applications)
key_sources: John Chick, Laura Morello and Stephanie Staffey. (2026). From fear to innovation: a case study of transformative faculty development for ethical AI integration in higher education. International Journal for Educational Integrity. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40979-026-00225-x

article_title: Estimating Learners' Skill Acquisition Without Temporal Information
citation: Ryosuke Nagai, Kyohei Atarashi, Koh Takeuchi, Jill-Jênn Vie, and Hisashi Kashima. (2026). Estimating Learners' Skill Acquisition Without Temporal Information. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20611
title: Neural expected-increment model with Upper Bounded Softmax for next-skill prediction
description: The article introduces a feed-forward neural model that maps a continuous mastery state to a distribution over the next skill using the Upper Bounded Softmax function, which assigns probability mass only to currently unmastered skills. Parameters are trained by minimizing squared reconstruction error of observed mastery patterns with L1 regularization that "promotes sparse and interpretable dependencies among skills." Repeatedly accumulating expected increments approximates intermediate acquisition states.
requirements: Continuous intermediate state representations relaxed from binary mastery patterns
Output constrained to the simplex intersected with unmastered skills
constraints: Direct path enumeration is infeasible as the number of possible acquisition paths grows exponentially, so complete paths are not modeled
target_learners: Learners assessed via cognitive diagnostic models in snapshot settings
target_learning_goals: Predicting the conditional distribution of the next acquired skill
examples: The model reconstructs each observed mastery pattern by applying the state update as many times as skills mastered
key_sources: Ryosuke Nagai, Kyohei Atarashi, Koh Takeuchi, Jill-Jênn Vie, and Hisashi Kashima. (2026). Estimating Learners' Skill Acquisition Without Temporal Information. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20611

article_title: A Multi-Temporal Context-aware System for Competences Management
citation: João H. Rosa, Jorge L. V. Barbosa, Marcos Kich, Lucas Brito. (2015). A Multi-Temporal Context-aware System for Competences Management. Int J Artif Intell Educ 25:455–492. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0047-y
title: UbiTrail model for generic trails management, chosen over Life Annotation, PELEP and Hong et al.'s mechanism
description: UbiTrail (Silva et al. 2010) is the trail-management model MultCComp adopts for its past dimension. A trail is a sequence of ptrail registers with attributes entity, resources, event, extension and location, based on the UbiTrail ontology; its architecture comprises a UbiTrailServer storing trails and providing basic and specialized services, and a UbiTrailClient running on users' mobile devices. The article compares it with three alternatives: 'Life Annotation ... does not standardize the trails information, which makes it difficult to query them'; PELEP 'does not support generic trails management'; and Hong et al.'s mechanism 'does not support the creation of services to query the trails'.
requirements: Applications must specify the ontology for their domain before using UbiTrail
constraints: UbiTrail assumes external providers of context and location data
target_learners: workers and learners in context-aware environments whose activity histories are managed
target_learning_goals: recording and querying learners'/workers' past activities to support personalized services
examples: MultCComp uses UbiTrail to store ptrail records whenever workers perform competence-development activities, and the Competences Agent queries the trails to infer developed competences
key_sources: João H. Rosa, Jorge L. V. Barbosa, Marcos Kich, Lucas Brito. (2015). A Multi-Temporal Context-aware System for Competences Management. Int J Artif Intell Educ 25:455–492. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0047-y

article_title: Mental health, resilience, and academic outcomes among university students: a global scoping review with particular attention to African and Global South contexts.
citation: Zhandire, T. T., Bakare-Fatungase, O. D., & Mkhize, N. (2026). Mental health, resilience, and academic outcomes among university students: a global scoping review with particular attention to African and Global South contexts. BMC Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40359-026-05242-6
title: Ubuntu-informed relational resilience as a framework for student mental health research
description: The review advances an Ubuntu-informed framework, grounded in the aphorism umuntu ngumuntu ngabantu ("a person is a person through other persons"), in which "resilience is not a personal trait to be measured on a scale but a communal process enacted through mutual care, intergenerational relationships, spiritual grounding, and collective solidarity". It extends socio-ecological models by grounding resilience explicitly in African relational values. The review uses it as an epistemological lens identifying what existing evidence renders invisible.
requirements: Operationalisation of relational and communal dimensions in instrument development, intervention design, and theoretical modelling rather than rhetorical use of Ubuntu.
constraints: The review reports that no study in the eligible literature employed Ubuntu or any African philosophical framework as a primary theoretical lens.
target_learners: undergraduate university students in African and Global South higher education contexts
target_learning_goals: understanding and supporting student resilience, mental health, and academic persistence
examples: The review's findings are informing an ongoing empirical study at the University of KwaZulu-Natal in which measurement instruments have been contextually adapted.
key_sources: Zhandire, T. T., Bakare-Fatungase, O. D., & Mkhize, N. (2026). Mental health, resilience, and academic outcomes among university students: a global scoping review with particular attention to African and Global South contexts. BMC Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40359-026-05242-6

article_title: Impact of Backward Design on Improving Iranian Advanced Learners' Writing Ability: Teachers' Practices and Beliefs
citation: Hosseini, H., Chalak, A., & Biria, R. (2019). Impact of Backward Design on Improving Iranian Advanced Learners’ Writing Ability: Teachers’ Practices and Beliefs. International Journal of Instruction, 12(2), 33-50. https://doi.org/10.29333/iji.2019.1223a
title: Understanding by Design (UbD) backward design framework
description: The article describes UbD as a planning model championed by Wiggins and McTighe (1998) in which curriculum is designed "backward" from desired results. At its core, UbD has three main stages: "(a) Identify the desired results, (b) determine the desired evidence, and (c) plan instruction and experiences to meet the results". The framework rests on seven key tenets, including teaching for understanding and transfer, six facets of understanding (explain, interpret, apply, shift perspective, empathize, self-assess), teachers as coaches of understanding, and regular review of units against design standards. The article applies this model as the experimental writing-instruction treatment.
requirements: Effective curriculum is planned backward from long-term desired results through the three-stage design process (Desired Results, Evidence, and Learning Plan)
constraints: The article notes the framework helps planning "without offering a rigid process or prescriptive recipe"
examples: The experimental group in this study was taught IELTS writing through the backward design while the control group received conventional forward design instruction
key_sources: Hosseini, H., Chalak, A., & Biria, R. (2019). Impact of Backward Design on Improving Iranian Advanced Learners’ Writing Ability: Teachers’ Practices and Beliefs. International Journal of Instruction, 12(2), 33-50. https://doi.org/10.29333/iji.2019.1223a

article_title: Understanding by Design (UbD) in EFL Teaching: The Investigation of Students' Foreign Language Learning Motivation and Views
citation: Yurtseven, N., & Altun, S. (2015). The Investigation of the Impact of Understanding by Design (UbD) on EFL Teaching: Students' Foreign Language Learning Motivation and Views. Journal of Education and Training Studies, 4(3). https://doi.org/10.11114/jets.v4i3.1204
title: Understanding by Design (UbD) and its backward design approach
description: Understanding by Design is a unit-design framework in which teachers act as designers who plan for meaningful, transferable learning rather than content coverage. It is dominated by the backward design approach, in which teachers determine which evidences they want to reach before planning what and how to teach. The framework consists of three stages: desired results, evidence, and learning plan, using GRASPS performance-task criteria and WHERETO principles. In this study, teachers integrated UbD into EFL Reading and Listening & Speaking courses to target student motivation and knowledge transfer.
requirements: Teachers are trained about UbD before designing units
Designs stick to the current curriculum's objectives while enriching content via UbD's guiding principles such as big idea, essential questions, performance tasks, and differentiation
constraints: The study was carried out at a university's preparatory classes for Reading and Listening & Speaking courses only
target_learners: University preparatory-class EFL students at A, B, and C proficiency levels
examples: Teachers formed four design groups, each designing three unit plans per semester and implementing them in their classes, with evaluation meetings reshaping subsequent designs
key_sources: Yurtseven, N., & Altun, S. (2015). The Investigation of the Impact of Understanding by Design (UbD) on EFL Teaching: Students' Foreign Language Learning Motivation and Views. Journal of Education and Training Studies, 4(3). https://doi.org/10.11114/jets.v4i3.1204

article_title: Facilitator-guided vs self-guided debriefing in immersive virtual reality paediatric emergency training: a randomised pilot study on learning outcomes and feasibility.
citation: Sohlin Amalie Middelboe, Hoffmann Ida Madeline, Poulsen Anja, Gjærde Line Klingen, Chang Todd P., Lee Joy Yeonjoo, Overbeck Gritt, Lund Stine, Sørensen Jette Led, Kjærgaard Jesper. (2026). Facilitator-guided vs self-guided debriefing in immersive virtual reality paediatric emergency training: a randomised pilot study on learning outcomes and feasibility. European Journal of Pediatrics. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00431-026-06898-3
title: UbiSim immersive VR multiplayer paediatric emergency scenarios with Oculus Quest 2
description: Four immersive VR scenarios simulating paediatric emergency cases (sepsis, increased intracranial pressure, respiratory distress, anaphylaxis) built into UbiSim's immersive VR platform and delivered on Oculus Quest 2 headsets. Trainee doctor-nurse dyads collaborate as avatars to stabilise a virtual patient whose condition "changed dynamically based on predefined responses in vital signs and clinical presentation". Interaction points and dropdown menus let trainees initiate evaluation and treatment; teleportation enables movement. Each scenario lasted 15–20 min followed by a 20-min debriefing.
requirements: VR headsets and the UbiSim platform; the article notes brief assistance was needed to access the correct app and scenario, and technical support and backup headsets were important
constraints: Five headsets failed to log into the scenario module on the first day, requiring adaptation; 46% of participants reported some cybersickness
examples: Dyads completed four interactive multiplayer VR scenarios over 4 h, with one dyad adapting by having the nurse in VR and the doctor supervising via computer screen during headset failure
key_sources: Sohlin Amalie Middelboe, Hoffmann Ida Madeline, Poulsen Anja, Gjærde Line Klingen, Chang Todd P., Lee Joy Yeonjoo, Overbeck Gritt, Lund Stine, Sørensen Jette Led, Kjærgaard Jesper. (2026). Facilitator-guided vs self-guided debriefing in immersive virtual reality paediatric emergency training: a randomised pilot study on learning outcomes and feasibility.
